blocks.text: We can represent the strength of a magnetic field B by lines of force in the same way as for an electric field. Then the population of these lines per unit area passing through a surface perpendicular to the field represents the magnetic flux.

blocks.title: Magnetic flux
blocks.text: The magnetic flux through a patch of area A is the number of magnetic lines passing through this area. If B represents the number of lines passing through unit area placed perpendicular to the field, then B = phi/A ... (10.4).

The surface A may not be perpendicular to the field; that is, the normal to the surface may make an angle theta with B (Fig. 10.5). Then we use the component of B (B cos theta) along the vector area A (Fig. 10.6). Therefore the flux passing through the surface is phi_B = BA cos theta ... (10.5). As B and A are both vectors, we can write phi_B = B.A ... (10.6). Equation 10.6 shows that phi_B is a scalar quantity: the magnetic flux phi_B through a plane element of area A in a uniform magnetic field B is given by the dot product of B and A.

blocks.alt: Parallel blue lines of a uniform magnetic field B pass through a tilted orange area. The area's normal vector A makes angle theta with B. A box gives the flux = B . A = B A cos theta, where B cos theta is the part of B along A.
blocks.caption: Flux through an area tilted in a field: flux = B A cos theta (original diagram after Figures 10.5 and 10.6).

blocks.text: A is a vector whose magnitude is the area of the element and whose direction is along the normal to the surface of the element, and theta is the angle between the directions of B and A (Fig. 10.5). In Fig. 10.7(a) the field is directed along the normal to the area, so theta is zero (cos 0 = 1) and the flux is maximum, equal to BA. When the field is parallel to the plane of the area (Fig. 10.7b), the angle between the field and the normal is 90 degrees (cos 90 = 0), so the flux through the area in this orientation is zero. For a curved surface in a uniform field, the surface is divided into a number of small elements, each assumed plane, and the flux through the whole surface is the sum of the contributions of all the elements using Eq. 10.5.

blocks.alt: Two panels with the same horizontal magnetic field. (a) A loop faces the field, its normal A along B: the most field lines pass and the flux is B A. (b) The loop lies along the field, its normal at 90 degrees to B: no lines pass and the flux is zero.
blocks.caption: Flux is maximum (a) when B is along the normal and zero (b) when B is parallel to the area (original diagram after Figure 10.7).

blocks.title: Weber and flux density
blocks.text: From the definition of the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux is N m A^-1, which is called the weber (Wb). According to Eq. 10.5 the magnetic induction B is the flux per unit area of a surface perpendicular to B; hence it is also called the magnetic flux density, with unit Wb m^-2. Therefore the magnetic field strength is measured in Wb m^-2 or N A^-1 m^-1 (tesla).

blocks.title: Example 10.2
blocks.text: A rectangular loop of wire, 25 cm long and 20 cm wide, is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 1.2 T. Determine the magnetic flux through the loop for the three orientations shown in Fig. 10.8 (cited as Fig. 10.9 in print), where the loop makes 30, 45 and 60 degrees with the field. Solution: A = 20 cm x 25 cm = 5 x 10^-2 m^2. (a) The angle between B and the area vector A is theta = 60 degrees: phi_B = BA cos theta = 1.2 T x 5 x 10^-2 m^2 x 0.5 = 3 x 10^-2 Wb. (b) theta = 45 degrees: phi_B = 1.2 x 5 x 10^-2 x 0.707 = 4.2 x 10^-2 Wb. (c) theta = 30 degrees: phi_B = 1.2 x 5 x 10^-2 x 0.866 = 5.2 x 10^-2 Wb.

blocks.alt: Three panels of the same loop in a horizontal field. With its normal A along B (theta = 0) the flux is B A; at theta = 60 degrees it is B A cos 60, half as much; at theta = 90 degrees, with the loop lying along the field, the flux is zero.
blocks.caption: One loop at 0, 60 and 90 degrees to the field (Example 10.2) (original diagram after Figures 10.8 and 10.9).
Flux through a plane area
header: Angle theta between B and the normal

blocks.prompt: Distinguish between magnetic flux and flux density. How are they related (comprehensive question 10.1)? A magnetic field is necessary for flux through a coil, yet a field does not guarantee flux through it; account for this (short question 10.9).
blocks.explanation: Flux phi_B = B.A is a scalar, the number of field lines through an area, in webers; flux density B is a vector, the flux per unit area through a surface held perpendicular to the field, in Wb m^-2 (tesla); they are related by phi_B = BA cos theta, or B = phi/A for a perpendicular area. If the plane of the coil lies along the field, the angle between B and the normal is 90 degrees and cos 90 = 0, so no flux passes through the coil even though the field is there.

items: Magnetic flux: number of field lines through an area; B = phi/A (10.4); phi_B = BA cos theta (10.5) = B.A (10.6), a scalar; maximum when the area faces the field, zero when it lies along it; curved surfaces are split into small plane elements.
Unit of flux: weber, 1 Wb = 1 N m A^-1; B is the flux density, 1 T = 1 Wb m^-2 = 1 N A^-1 m^-1. Example 10.2: 3.0, 4.2 and 5.2 x 10^-2 Wb.
